## What it is

The line is Charles Margossian's. He said it in a work meeting about a feature of the Stan software (embedded Laplace approximations): making it more flexible would complicate the interface. Gelman relates it to "the well-known tension between freedom and security in politics, or the tension between freedom and regularization in statistical inference", and then turns it around. In the 8 schools example, the no-pooling model has the most freedom in one sense, but "in another sense, the hierarchical model gives you more freedom because it regularizes away the worst excesses of the fit", like a trapeze artist with a net. "Ultimately, for statistical software the most user friendly thing is for it to enable users to do useful analyses."

Flexible tools such as probabilistic programming languages let you fit almost any model. That freedom has a price: you make decisions that a constrained, "user-friendly" tool would have made for you, and every one is a chance to get something wrong.

## Why it matters

There's a real tension in tool design. Constrained software with sensible defaults protects novices from many mistakes but stops experts from building the right model. Flexible software lets experts do excellent work and lets novices produce elaborate nonsense. Neither is better in general. The right choice depends on who is using the tool and how much support, such as defaults, checks and workflow guidance, comes with the freedom.

## How it works

A toy model. Analysis quality depends on matching the model to the problem. A **constrained** tool offers a few good default models, so its quality is moderate and fairly consistent regardless of skill. A **free** tool lets the analyst specify any model. Quality then depends on skill: experts land near the best model, and novices scatter widely, sometimes far below the constrained tool's floor.

## Simulated example

Simulate many analysts of varying skill using either a constrained or a free tool. Compare the distributions of analysis quality.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, quantile, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof skill = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Average analyst skill"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 102, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
freedom = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  return range(2000).flatMap(() => {
    const s = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, r.normal(skill, 0.2)));
    const constrained = 0.65 + r.normal(0, 0.05);                 // good defaults, limited ceiling
    const free = 0.95 - (1 - s) * Math.abs(r.normal(0, 0.6));     // ceiling high, floor depends on skill
    return [{tool: "Constrained, user-friendly", q: constrained}, {tool: "Free, flexible", q: Math.max(-0.5, free)}];
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "Freedom: simulation chart",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: Analysis quality (1 = best possible). Vertical axis: Analysts. The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 280,
  facet: {data: freedom, y: "tool", marginRight: 160},
  x: {label: "Analysis quality (1 = best possible)", domain: [-0.5, 1]},
  y: {label: "Analysts", grid: true},
  marks: [Plot.rectY(freedom, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "q", fill: "tool", thresholds: 40, domain: [-0.5, 1]})), Plot.ruleY([0])],
  color: {range: ["#8a8a8a", "#2166ac"]}
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const q = (t, p) => quantile(freedom.filter(d => d.tool === t).map(d => d.q), p);
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`Median quality: constrained **${fmt(q("Constrained, user-friendly", 0.5))}**, free **${fmt(q("Free, flexible", 0.5))}**. Worst 10%: constrained ${fmt(q("Constrained, user-friendly", 0.1))}, free ${fmt(q("Free, flexible", 0.1))}. Raise the skill slider and freedom pays off. Lower it and the user-friendly tool wins. Freedom isn't user-friendly.`}</div>`;
}
```

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# Freedom: it's not user friendly.
skill <- 0.5 # average analyst skill # <1>
set.seed(102) # <2>

s <- pmin(1, pmax(0, rnorm(2000, skill, 0.2))) # each analyst
constrained <- 0.65 + rnorm(2000, 0, 0.05) # good defaults, limited ceiling # <3>
free <- pmax(-0.5, 0.95 - (1 - s) * abs(rnorm(2000, 0, 0.6))) # skill-bound # <4>

q <- rbind(
  constrained = quantile(constrained, c(0.1, 0.5)),
  free = quantile(free, c(0.1, 0.5))
)
print(round(q, 2)) # worst 10% and median quality

boxplot( # <5>
  list(
    "Constrained, user-friendly" = constrained,
    "Free, flexible" = free
  ),
  col = c("#2166ac", "#d6604d"), ylab = "Quality of the analysis"
)
```
1. The page's control: the average skill of the analysts.
2. Fixes the random numbers so the run is reproducible.
3. A constrained, user-friendly tool: good defaults, a limited ceiling, hard to misuse.
4. A free, flexible tool: a higher ceiling, but the floor depends on the analyst's skill.
5. The two distributions of analysis quality. Freedom raises the best outcomes and lowers the worst.

## Python {.unlisted}

```{.python}
# Freedom: it's not user friendly.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

skill = 0.5  # average analyst skill
rng = np.random.default_rng(102)

s = np.clip(rng.normal(skill, 0.2, 2000), 0, 1)          # each analyst
constrained = 0.65 + rng.normal(0, 0.05, 2000)  # good defaults, low ceiling
free = np.maximum(-0.5, 0.95 - (1 - s) * np.abs(rng.normal(0, 0.6, 2000)))

for name, q in [("Constrained", constrained), ("Free", free)]:
    print(f"{name}: median quality {np.median(q):.2f}, "
          f"worst 10% {np.quantile(q, 0.1):.2f}")

plt.boxplot([constrained, free], patch_artist=True)
plt.xticks([1, 2], ["Constrained, user-friendly", "Free, flexible"])
plt.ylabel("Quality of the analysis")
plt.show()
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Flexibility lets you build the right model, and lets you build very wrong ones.
- Constrained tools set a floor on quality. Free tools raise the ceiling.
- Good flexible tools come with good defaults, checks and workflow guidance.
:::
